verses.translation_literal: Come, let us sing out to YHWH; let us shout in triumph to the rock of our salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come! Let the singing begin, and let it be for the LORD. Let the shout go up, a great ringing cry, to the Rock who saves us.
verses.directors_commentary: The opening word is 'go', not 'come': Hebrew uses 'go' as a nudge to act, 'up, let's do it', as Radak and Meiri note (compare Gen 19:32, 37:20). This is a crowd at a gate or procession, one voice turning to the next. The two verbs are different noises: rnn is a ringing, sung cry; rw' (hari'a) is the teru'ah, the loud shout of acclamation that greets a king, a victory or the ark's arrival (1 Sam 4:5). KJV's 'make a joyful noise' for the second verb is right in spirit but flattens the word into a hymn; it is closer to a war-cry turned to praise. 'Rock' (tsur) is a title for God as a fortress in a land of cliffs and caves, a refuge from raiders and sun, and it quietly displaces the rock-and-stone deities of neighbouring cults.

philological_notes.note: To raise the teru'ah, the shout of acclamation or alarm; used for the arrival of a king or the ark. Not merely 'noise'.
Rock, cliff; as a title of God, the unshakable refuge.

verses.translation_literal: Let us come before his face with thanksgiving; with songs let us shout in triumph to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let us go to meet his face, and let thanks be what we carry in our hands. With songs, with songs, let us raise the shout for him.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Come before' is the verb qdm, 'to go ahead of, to meet', with a sense of getting there first and arriving ready (Radak: 'prepare ourselves'). 'His face' is the idiom for presence: one comes to the shrine to 'see the face' of God. The thank-offering and its song (todah) were done in public, in the temple court, with the whole community watching. KJV 'psalms' is a Greek-derived word for what Hebrew calls zemirot, simply 'songs' or 'sung music'. The structure matters: the verse ends with 'shout to him', the same verb as verse 1, so the opening and the close of the call to worship mirror one another.

philological_notes.note: To come to meet, to be ahead of; here to present oneself before God.
Thanksgiving, public acknowledgment of what God has done, also the name of a thank-offering.

verses.translation_literal: For a great God [is] YHWH, and a great king over all gods.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD is God, and great. He is a king, and great, above every power men have ever called a god.
verses.directors_commentary: Here is the reason ('for') for all the singing. The Hebrew puts 'great God' first and 'YHWH' after it: not 'the LORD is a great God' but 'a great God is YHWH', as YLT keeps it. The pair 'great God, great king' is treaty language: a Great King is a suzerain over lesser kings, and the 'gods' (elohim) here are the lesser rulers beneath him. KJV's 'above all gods' is correct, but the audience would hear polemic: the gods of Canaan, Egypt and Babylon are the vassals, not the rivals. The medieval commentators read these elohim as angels or the heavenly host (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David); the text itself does not say, and it does not need to.

philological_notes.note: 'Great King' is the title of an overlord in ancient Near Eastern treaties; here it is applied to YHWH over the lesser 'gods'.
Plural: 'gods' or heavenly beings. Medieval commentators read angels.

verses.translation_literal: Who [has] in his hand the depths of earth, and the peaks of the mountains [are] his.
verses.translation_dramatic: In his hand lie the deep places of the earth, down where no one has been. And the high peaks, standing in the thin air, are his as well.
verses.directors_commentary: A merism: from the lowest to the highest, so everything between belongs to him. 'Depths' (mechqere) is from the root 'to search out', so literally 'the searched-out things', the places only explorers and miners would plumb, which means that the deepest place a person could reach is still in his hand. The second word is the hard one, ta'afot. KJV's 'strength of the hills' follows one old derivation; Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it to the root for flying, 'the heights', and that fits the contrast with depths. Mountains were also where the Canaanite gods were thought to live, so 'the peaks are his' takes them away from the neighbours' pantheon.

philological_notes.note: 'Things searched out', the depths; Radak compares Jer 31:37 'the foundations of the earth searched out below'.
Rare. Either 'heights' (from flying, Rashi), 'strength' (KJV, Ibn Ezra), or 'shining' (Meiri). Heights is best here, set against 'depths'.

verses.translation_literal: Whose [is] the sea, and he made it, and the dry land his hands formed.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sea is his, the restless sea, and he is the one who made it. And the dry land, firm under our feet, his own hands shaped it.
verses.directors_commentary:
For a people who feared the sea as the home of chaos, this is a bold claim: the sea is not a rival power but a possession. The line has a built-in contrast. The sea is his, and he made it, with a plain verb; the dry land his hands formed, with a potter's verb (yatsar) and the hands put first for emphasis. Play the second half slower and warmer, as a craftsman's work.

The idea of dry land recalls Gen 1:9-10, where God gathers the waters and calls the dry land 'earth'. But the word there is yabbashah; yabbeshet is rare, found here and in Exod 4:9 (the Nile water turning to 'dry land'). Meiri notes that it comes in the absolute form rather than the usual construct. The KJV 'his hands formed the dry land' is faithful, but it hides the order of the Hebrew, which keeps 'sea' and 'dry land' as the two poles of the world, as Ibn Ezra says in reading them as one globe. The verb 'made' also carries a hint of putting in order, as Metzudat David and Radak read it: he set the waters in one place.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun for 'dry land', found here and Exod 4:9. It recalls Gen 1:9-10, which uses yabbashah, but it is a different form, and it stands in the absolute where a construct is expected.
The verb of the potter, 'to form, shape'. It is plural ('they formed') with 'hands' as subject, and it sets the shaping of the land against the plain 'made' for the sea.

verses.translation_literal: Come in, let us bow down and bend low; let us kneel before YHWH our maker.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come in. Let us bow down, let us bend low, let us go down on our knees before the LORD, who made us.
verses.directors_commentary: The tone shifts from shouting to stillness: the verbs of the first half are about voice; these are about bodies. 'Come in' (bo'u) is a different verb from verse 1's 'go': here the crowd is at the threshold and entering the sanctuary. The three verbs are three postures, which Radak and Metzudat David define: hishtachavah, lying prostrate full length; kara', bending the head and upper body; and barakh, from berekh, 'knee', going down on the knees. KJV's 'worship' for the first loses the physical act, and its 'kneel' is right; but it also reads as if all three are the same. The Hebrew choreography is a descent. Note too that barakh here is not 'bless', a homonym (Rashi cites Gen 24:11, the camels made to kneel).

philological_notes.note: To bow down, prostrate oneself; Radak and Metzudat David define it as lying flat with the whole body.
'Let us kneel', from berekh 'knee', not 'bless'.
'Our maker'. Metzudat Zion reads the verb as 'raised up, made great', as in Deut 32:6; the plain sense of the root is 'make'.

verses.translation_literal: For he [is] our God, and we [are] the people of his pasture and the flock of his hand. Today, if to his voice you listen,
verses.translation_dramatic: For he is our God, and we are the people he leads to pasture, the flock held in his hand. Then the voice turns and looks straight at you. Today. If you will listen to his voice...
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'for' gives the reason for the bowing in v6: because he is our God. The shepherd image is not soft. A flock depends on the shepherd's hand for water, for direction and for safety, and Metzudat David reads 'flock of his hand' as the gentle shepherd who guides by a motion of the hand and not with the rod. The KJV renders 'the sheep of his hand', which is close, but it makes 'pasture' a possessive ('his pasture') where the Hebrew says the people whom he pastures, as Radak reads it.

Then comes the turn. Until now the speaker has said 'we'; at 'today' he says 'you', and the call to worship becomes a warning. God's own first-person voice does not enter until v9 ('they tested me'). The clause is left open: 'if you listen' has no ending. The KJV and Webster leave it so, while the ASV and BBE turn it into a wish ('oh that you would'). Keep the silence after 'listen'. Radak hears in it a warning not to be like the wilderness generation, who tested God at Rephidim and Meribah. 'Today' is not a date; it is every day a hearer stands in the temple court.

philological_notes.note: 'His pasture', the place and care of grazing. The shepherd image sits in the noun itself: the people are the ones he feeds and leads. Radak reads it as the shepherd who has led us up to now.
'Today', with the article. It marks the point where the voice turns from 'we' to 'you'. Rashi takes it as 'in this world'; Ibn Ezra joins it to the call 'come, let us bow down today'.

verses.translation_literal: Do not harden your heart like Meribah, like the day of Massah in the wilderness,
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not harden your hearts, as they did at Meribah, as on that day at Massah in the wilderness.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Heart' here is the singular for a plural 'you': a whole people with one heart. KJV translates the place names as common nouns, 'the provocation' and 'the day of temptation', and so loses that the audience knew them as sites: Meribah means 'quarrel', Massah 'testing', and both names come from one story (Exod 17:7, where Israel asked 'Is YHWH among us or not?'). The Hebrew has no 'in': it is 'like Meribah, like the day of Massah', so the place is made into a type of behaviour. 'Harden' is from qashah, 'hard, stiff', the same word as a 'stiff neck'. The warning is the pivot of the psalm: the voice that began in song now speaks as God, and what follows is a history lesson addressed to the present.

philological_notes.note: 'Quarrel'; a place name (Exod 17:7) and also a common noun, which KJV renders 'provocation'.
'Testing'; the second name given to the same place (Exod 17:7). Metzudat David says the two names are one event.

verses.translation_literal: When your fathers tested me, they tried me, though they had seen my work.
verses.translation_dramatic: That was where your fathers put me to the test. They tried me, even though they had seen what I had done.
verses.directors_commentary: God now speaks in the first person ('me', 'my'), with no 'thus says the LORD': the psalm slides into the divine voice. 'Tested' and 'tried' are two verbs, nasah and bachan, nearly synonyms; the second is the word for assaying metal, so Israel is putting God in the crucible, the judged turned judge. KJV's 'tempted' is the weak spot: in 1611 it meant 'tested', but today it suggests an invitation to sin. The last clause has 'gam' (also, even): 'even though they had seen', so the sin is worse because it followed the signs. Rashi places those sights in Egypt; Radak adds the sea, the manna and the water from the rock.

philological_notes.note: 'Put me to the test'; in Exod 17 the people try God by demanding water.
'Assayed me'; the verb is used for testing metal.

token_glosses.gloss: they put me to the test

verses.translation_literal: Forty years I loathed a generation, and I said: A people straying of heart, they; and they, they did not know my ways.
verses.translation_dramatic: Forty years I could not stand that generation. I said: They are a people whose hearts wander. They, they have never known my ways.
verses.directors_commentary: Forty years is the length of the wilderness wandering, a generation's span. The verb aqut means 'to feel disgust', as one does at something that makes the stomach turn (Rashi cites Job 10:1, 'my soul is disgusted with my life'); Radak and Metzudat Zion take it from 'quarrel'. KJV 'grieved' is milder than the Hebrew: this is loathing, not sorrow. KJV also adds 'this generation', but the Hebrew has only 'a generation'. Then the diagnosis: 'straying of heart', their hearts wander as a stray animal does, and the repeated 'they, and they' points a finger. 'Ways' (derakhim) are his paths and his way of acting: they did not understand how he works, which is the shepherd metaphor again in the negative.

philological_notes.note: 'I loathed, was disgusted with'; the root also occurs in Ezek 6:9 and Job 10:1. Others derive it from 'quarrel'.
'Strayers of heart', those whose hearts wander like lost sheep; compare Ps 119:176.

verses.translation_literal: So that I swore in my anger: If they shall enter into my rest...
verses.translation_dramatic: And so I swore, in my anger: They shall never enter my rest.
verses.directors_commentary: The ending is cut short on purpose. 'If they shall enter my rest' is half of an oath: the speaker stops before the curse that would follow, and everyone knows it means 'may such-and-such happen to me if they enter', so 'they never will'. Radak and Metzudat David say so, and compare Ps 89:36. KJV supplies 'that they should not enter', which is correct in sense but removes the sharpness of an oath left unfinished. 'Anger' is literally 'nose' (af), the nose that flares. 'Rest' (menuchah) is the land and settled life after the wandering (Radak, Deut 12:9), and for Rashi the land and Jerusalem (Ps 132:14). The psalm began with 'come in' and ends with the door shut on those who would not listen, and the 'today' of verse 7 leaves it open to the audience.

philological_notes.note: Oath formula: 'if they enter' with the curse left unspoken, meaning 'they shall surely not enter'.
'My rest': the land of promise, settled life after wandering; for Rashi also Jerusalem.
